standard_prerequisites: Cartesian product types with their induction principle: to construct or prove something about arbitrary elements it suffices to consider pairs.
The action of the projections on paths: ap of the first and second projection applied to a path in the product.
The induction principle for identity types (path induction) with its conversion rule.
The notion of quasi-inverse of a function.
core_obligations: Construct the function from pairs of component paths back to a path in the product type.
Prove that the function from paths in the product to pairs of component paths and the constructed inverse are quasi-inverse to each other.
Conclude that the canonical function from x = y to the pair of component path types is an equivalence.
proof_roadmap: Define the candidate inverse by product induction: assume x and y are pairs (a, b) and (a-prime, b-prime); by induction on the components reduce to the case where both component paths are reflexivity; output reflexivity of the pair.

First quasi-inverse direction: given r in the path type of the product, induct on r to reduce to reflexivity; the projection actions compute on reflexivity so the forward map sends it to the pair of reflexivity paths; then induct on the pair components to see the inverse returns reflexivity, which is r under the current assumptions.

Second quasi-inverse direction: given a pair s of component paths, induct on the endpoints to make them pairs, induct on s to split it into component paths, then induct on the components to reduce them to reflexivity; the inverse produces reflexivity of the pair and the forward map returns the original pair of reflexivity paths.
Conclude the equivalence: the two maps are quasi-inverse, so the canonical function is an equivalence.
difficulty_reason: A quadruple induction argument with careful ordering ('they have to be done in the right order' per the author) to establish both quasi-inverse directions.
